items.title: Valid Parentheses

solutionCode.label: push openers, match the top on every closer

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) worst case (all openers).

followups.q: Why does "([)]" fail but "()[]" pass?
followups.a: Both have matching counts, so a counter cannot tell them apart. The stack enforces nesting: at the ")" the top is "[", the wrong opener, so it rejects. Nesting is a structural constraint, and only a stack records which bracket is innermost.

followups.q: What are the three distinct failure modes?
followups.a: A closer arriving with an empty stack ("]"), a closer whose top is the wrong type ("([)]"), and leftover openers at the end ("(["). All three need their own check — dropping any one accepts an invalid string.

items.title: Implement Queue using Stacks

solutionCode.label: flip-on-empty: never flip while the out stack still has work

items.complexity: push O(1). pop and peek are amortised O(1): every element moves between the stacks exactly once in its lifetime. Worst-case single call is O(n).

followups.q: State the flip-on-empty law and why it matters.
followups.a: Only flip when the out stack is empty. Flipping while out still holds elements would interleave newer items ahead of older ones and break FIFO. The law is what keeps the two stacks a correct queue, not just a fast one.

followups.q: Give the amortised argument.
followups.a: Each element is pushed to in once, moved to out once, and popped from out once — three constant-time operations over its whole lifetime. So n operations cost O(n) total, giving O(1) amortised, even though one individual pop can move n elements.

items.title: Implement Stack using Queues
hints: push: enqueue then rotate size-1 times front→back.

solutionCode.label: one queue, rotated after every push so the newest sits in front

items.complexity: push O(n) — one rotation per push. pop, top and empty are O(1). The cost is deliberately front-loaded so removal stays cheap.

followups.q: Why put the cost in push rather than pop?
followups.a: Either works, but concentrating it in push means the queue always holds elements in stack order, so pop, top and empty are trivial O(1) reads. The two-queue version spreads the cost differently but is not asymptotically better — total work is the same.

followups.q: Why does the loop run size()-1 times?
followups.a: You want every PREVIOUSLY present element moved behind the new one. After appending, the queue has size elements, of which size-1 are old. Rotating size times would move the new element too and undo the whole thing.

items.title: Min Stack (revisit + delta variant)

solutionCode.label: pair version, then the delta encoding that removes the second stack

items.complexity: All operations O(1). Pair version costs O(n) extra space; the delta encoding costs O(1) extra beyond the values themselves.

followups.q: Why is the encoded value guaranteed to be below the new minimum?
followups.a: Encoded = 2x - oldMin, and it is only written when x < oldMin. Then encoded - x = x - oldMin < 0, so encoded < x = the new minimum. That strict inequality is what lets top() and pop() recognise an encoded slot with a single comparison — no flag, no second stack.

followups.q: What is the delta version's hidden cost?
followups.a: Overflow. 2*x - oldMin can exceed int range when values sit near the extremes, so the stack must be wider than the values it holds. That is why the C++ version stores long long. The pair version has no such hazard, which is usually worth its extra memory.

items.title: Next Greater Element I
items.statement: nums1 queries into nums2's answers via map.

solutionCode.label: monotonic decreasing stack builds a value-to-answer map

items.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n). Each element of nums2 is pushed and popped at most once.

followups.q: Why is each element pushed and popped at most once?
followups.a: An element is pushed exactly when it is read, and popped only when a strictly greater element arrives — after which it never returns. So across the whole scan there are at most n pushes and n pops, giving O(n) despite the nested while loop. That amortisation is the monotonic stack's entire selling point.

followups.q: Why can the answers be keyed by value?
followups.a: The problem guarantees nums2 has distinct values and nums1 is a subset of it. With duplicates the map would collide and you would key by index instead, then locate each nums1 element first. Always check the distinctness guarantee before keying on values.

items.title: Next Greater Element II (circular)

solutionCode.label: walk 2n indices with modulo; only push during the first lap

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n). The doubled loop is 2n iterations, still linear.

followups.q: Why does the second lap not push?
followups.a: Every index already got its chance in lap one. Pushing again would leave stale indices on the stack that could be resolved twice, overwriting a correct earlier answer. The second lap exists only to RESOLVE leftovers by wrapping around, not to add new candidates.

followups.q: Why store indices rather than values?
followups.a: The answer must be written to out[originalIndex], and a value alone does not say where it came from — especially with duplicates. Indices also let you compute distances, which is exactly what Daily Temperatures needs.

solutionCode.label: same stack, but the answer is a distance rather than a value

followups.q: How is this different from Next Greater Element?
followups.a: Only the line inside the pop. NGE writes the value that resolved it; this writes i minus the popped index. Same stack, same invariant, different payload — which is why recognising the pattern matters more than memorising either problem.

followups.q: Why is the default 0 rather than -1?
followups.a: The answer is a wait time, and 0 correctly means "never gets warmer" in that unit. Using -1 would be a sentinel in the same numeric space as real answers, which is fine here but sloppier. Match the sentinel to the semantics of the value.

items.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates
hints: Push unless top equals char → pop instead.

solutionCode.label: the output itself is the stack; cascades fall out automatically

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the output stack.

followups.q: Why do cascades need no extra logic?
followups.a: After popping a pair, the new top is whatever preceded it, and the NEXT character is compared against that. On "abba", removing "bb" leaves "a" on top and the incoming "a" cancels it too. The stack automatically re-exposes the previous context — a scan-and-rebuild loop would need multiple passes.

followups.q: Why use the output string as the stack?
followups.a: Its back is the stack top, push_back and pop_back are O(1), and no copy is needed at the end. Using a separate stack then reversing it into a string is correct but does the same work twice.

items.title: Backspace String Compare
hints: Build helper per string; O(1)-space reverse-walk bonus.

solutionCode.label: build with a stack, plus the O(1)-space backward walk

items.complexity: Build version: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space. Reverse-walk version: O(n + m) time, O(1) space.

followups.q: Why walk backwards for the O(1) version?
followups.a: A backspace affects the character BEFORE it, so reading left to right you cannot know whether the current character survives until you have seen what follows. Reading right to left, each "#" is encountered before its victim, so a running skip counter is enough — no buffer needed.

followups.q: What does the guard on an empty buffer protect?
followups.a: A leading "#" deletes nothing. Without the guard, popping an empty stack throws in Python and is undefined behaviour in C++. LeetCode explicitly tests inputs like "##a", so it is a required case rather than defensive padding.

items.title: Infix → Postfix converter
items.statement: Full operator machine incl '^' right-assoc + parentheses.
hints: Section trace table is your spec.

solutionCode.label: shunting yard with precedence and right-associative exponent

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each token is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why does right-associativity change the pop condition?
followups.a: For left-associative operators, an equal-precedence operator on the stack must be emitted first so a-b-c becomes (a-b)-c. For right-associative "^", it must NOT be popped, so 2^3^2 stays 2^(3^2). The `!rightAssoc(c)` term is the entire difference, and it is the part most implementations get wrong.

followups.q: Why is the "(" never emitted to the output?
followups.a: Postfix encodes grouping in the operator order itself — parentheses carry no information once the expression is flattened. The "(" exists only as a barrier that stops the operator pops, and it is discarded when its matching ")" arrives.

items.title: Evaluate Postfix Expression

solutionCode.label: operand order matters: the SECOND pop is the left operand

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the operand stack.

followups.q: Why does the operand order matter so much?
followups.a: The stack returns the most recent operand first, which is the RIGHT-hand side. So b pops before a. For "+" and "*" the mistake is invisible because they commute; for "-" and "/" it silently produces the wrong sign or reciprocal. Every bug report on this problem is this line.

followups.q: Why int(a / b) rather than a // b in Python?
followups.a: Python's // floors toward negative infinity: -7 // 2 is -4. C, Java and most expression evaluators truncate toward zero: -7 / 2 is -3. Using // silently disagrees with the reference implementation on exactly the negative cases, which is what the test checks.
